tests.title: Extreme weather: changing storms and their impacts

groups.heading: Questions 1–3
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS for each answer.

questions.prompt: What people see and feel from day to day: the {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The opening distinction uses daily experience to explain weather.

questions.prompt: Climate is described in terms of the {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: Climate is contrasted with daily weather as a longer-term pattern.

questions.prompt: Conditions over which tropical storms form: warm tropical {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: Sarah describes these storms as forming over warm tropical waters.

groups.heading: Questions 4–6
groups.instruction: Choose the correct answer, A, B or C.
groups.answerInstruction: Choose ONE letter for each answer.

questions.prompt: What is the consequence of a storm remaining over an area for longer?

evidence.summary: The slower movement prolongs exposure to damaging wind and rainfall.

distractors.B: The account concerns prolonged strong winds rather than an immediate weakening.
distractors.C: Rain is described as lasting longer, not stopping.

options.label: A
options.text: The area experiences strong winds and rain for a longer time.

options.label: B
options.text: The winds must immediately become weaker.

options.label: C
options.text: The storm stops producing rainfall once it slows.

questions.prompt: What does greater likelihood of flooding mean here?

evidence.summary: The explanation treats likelihood as the probability of an event.

distractors.B: The term does not specify that flooding must wait until the storm leaves.

options.label: A
options.text: Flooding is guaranteed in every case.

options.label: B
options.text: Flooding will take place only after the storm has left.

options.label: C
options.text: Flooding becomes more probable.

questions.prompt: Which description matches the landslide and mudslide discussion?

evidence.summary: The account distinguishes downhill movement of earth or rock and rain-related mudslides from the later sea-water hazard.

distractors.A: Neither term is defined by wind stopping.
distractors.C: The landslide explanation specifies earth or rock; sea water belongs to the storm-surge discussion.

options.label: A
options.text: Both terms mean that wind has stopped blowing at sea.

options.label: B
options.text: Earth or rock can move rapidly down a slope, and heavy rain can precede mudslides.

options.label: C
options.text: Sea water is always the material that moves down the slope.

groups.answerInstruction: Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

evidence.summary: Darren describes sea water being swept inland during a storm surge.

questions.prompt: The danger could increase as sea levels are {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The account connects warming seas and rising sea levels with potentially more dangerous surges.

evidence.summary: Sarah states that storm surges can reach ten metres in height.

tests.title: Storm hazards: causes, mechanisms and averages

groups.heading: Questions 1–3
groups.instruction: Choose the correct answer, A, B or C.
groups.answerInstruction: Choose ONE letter for each answer.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes climate from weather in Sarah's explanation?

evidence.summary: Sarah distinguishes long-term climate from everyday weather conditions.

distractors.B: The distinction is temporal, not limited to oceans.
distractors.C: Daily weather is not restricted to destructive events.

options.label: A
options.text: Climate concerns a long-term pattern rather than the conditions experienced each day.

options.label: B
options.text: Climate concerns only conditions over the ocean.

options.label: C
options.text: Weather concerns only events that cause damage.

questions.prompt: Why are the names hurricane, cyclone and typhoon different?

evidence.summary: The naming distinction is geographical rather than three fundamentally different storm mechanisms.

distractors.A: The name is assigned by region rather than a later consequence such as landslides.
distractors.B: Sarah explicitly says they are actually the same.

options.label: A
options.text: The name indicates whether the storm has already caused a landslide.

options.label: B
options.text: The name identifies three unrelated types of weather.

options.label: C
options.text: The name depends on where the storm forms, although the storms are the same kind.

questions.prompt: Why can slower movement increase a storm's impact on one place?

evidence.summary: Longer local exposure to wind and rain explains the increased potential impact.

distractors.A: The storm's regional name is not determined by its speed.
distractors.C: The description says rain lasts longer and can cause more flooding.

options.label: A
options.text: A slow storm must immediately change from a cyclone into a hurricane.

options.label: B
options.text: The damaging conditions persist over the same area for longer.

options.label: C
options.text: Slower motion ensures that rain never reaches the ground.

evidence.summary: Rock is named alongside earth in the landslide definition.

questions.prompt: Weather condition that may precede a mudslide: particularly {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: Mudslides are associated with particularly heavy rainfall in the explanation.

tests.title: Regional differences and the consequences of warming

groups.heading: Questions 1–3
groups.answerInstruction: Write NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS for each answer.

evidence.summary: Sarah places climate on a long-term timescale in contrast with daily weather.

evidence.summary: The naming example associates the Atlantic with hurricanes.

questions.prompt: Which region is associated with typhoons? {{blank}}

evidence.summary: The West Pacific is the region Sarah names for typhoons.

groups.heading: Questions 4–6
groups.answerInstruction: Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

evidence.summary: The programme describes a projected increase in destructiveness as the world warms.

evidence.summary: Darren reports the view that storms are moving across areas more slowly.

questions.prompt: Remaining over one area means the rain will last for {{blank}}.

evidence.summary: The local duration of rainfall increases in the explanation of a slower storm.

groups.heading: Questions 7–8
groups.instruction: Choose the correct answer, A, B or C.
groups.answerInstruction: Choose ONE letter for each answer.

questions.prompt: What connection is made between climate change and storm-surge danger?

evidence.summary: The argument links warming seas and higher sea levels to potentially more dangerous storm surges.

distractors.A: Rainfall on slopes belongs to the earlier landslide discussion; surge danger concerns sea water.
distractors.C: The account describes a possible increase in danger, not a prevention of inland movement.

options.label: A
options.text: Storm surges are said to depend only on rainfall on a hillside.

options.label: B
options.text: Rising sea levels could make an already damaging storm component more dangerous.

options.label: C
options.text: Warming seas are said to prevent water from moving inland.

questions.prompt: Who is included when the programme explains casualties?

evidence.summary: The explanation covers both injury and loss of life.

distractors.B: Property damage alone is not the definition given for a casualty.
distractors.C: The definition includes injuries and does not impose this timing restriction.

options.label: A
options.text: People injured as well as people killed.

options.label: B
options.text: Only people whose homes were damaged but who were unharmed.

options.label: C
options.text: Only people who died at the exact moment a storm began.
